question: Technical round for a TCS Prime (NQT) role (campus-style drive, 4th July). The technical and managerial rounds were combined into a 25-minute session with no cross-questions. The second technical question was: **What is an abstract class?** Other questions included DBMS vs RDBMS, normalization and BCNF, insertion sort and removing spaces from a string.
lookingFor: Understanding of abstraction and how it differs from concrete classes and interfaces.
Knowing the rules of abstract classes in a specific language (Java or C++).
Ability to say when to use an abstract class versus an interface.
answer:
**Definition.** An **abstract class** is a class that **cannot be instantiated** and exists to be a base for other classes. It can contain **abstract (unimplemented) methods** that subclasses must implement, along with concrete methods and fields that subclasses inherit. It is a way to achieve **abstraction**: define *what* a group of classes must do and share some of *how*, while leaving specifics to subclasses.

**Java.**
```java
abstract class Shape {
    String color;                       // state is allowed
    Shape(String c) { color = c; }      // constructors are allowed (called via super)
    abstract double area();             // no body: subclasses must implement
    void describe() { System.out.println(color + " " + area()); }   // shared behaviour
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    Circle(String c, double r) { super(c); this.r = r; }
    double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
// Shape s = new Shape("red");   // compile error
Shape s = new Circle("red", 2);   // fine: reference of abstract type
```
Rules: declared with `abstract`; may have zero or more abstract methods (a class with an abstract method must itself be abstract); can have constructors, fields, static and final methods; a subclass must implement all abstract methods or be abstract itself; a class can extend only one class.

**C++.** A class is abstract if it has at least one **pure virtual function** (`virtual double area() = 0;`). It cannot be instantiated, but pointers and references to it are fine, which enables run-time polymorphism.

**Abstract class vs interface (Java).**
| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Inheritance | Single | Multiple |
| State (instance fields) | Yes | No (only constants) |
| Constructors | Yes | No |
| Methods | Abstract and concrete | Abstract, plus default and static methods |
| Use when | Related classes share code and state ("is-a") | Unrelated classes share a capability ("can-do") |

**Why use one.** It avoids duplicate code in related classes, enforces a contract, and lets you program against the abstract type, for example a `List<Shape>`.

**Common mistakes.** Trying to instantiate an abstract class, declaring an abstract method `private` or `final` (not allowed because it must be overridden), or using an abstract class when an interface would give needed flexibility.
